section_summary: This section assembles wartime assessments of Japan’s food position from 1942 through 1944, including British economic-warfare estimates, U.S. diplomatic reporting, cross-reference sheets, telegrams, and a lengthy Military Intelligence Service study. The documents examine rice stocks and rationing, imports from Japan’s empire and Southeast Asia, shipping vulnerability, fertilizer and farm-labor shortages, fisheries, soybeans, sugar, salt, and governmental food controls. The section concludes with the first part of a translated 1944 Japanese symposium in which agricultural officials acknowledge distribution problems and discuss fertilizer self-sufficiency, livestock feed, land improvement, seeds, fish, and soybeans.

subfiles.title: Confidential file identifier 894.5018/6
subfiles.about: Identifies a confidential file item under decimal classification 894.5018/6.
subfiles.summary: This single-page cover bears only the decimal-file number and a confidential-file designation. It contains no substantive correspondence or report text.

subfiles.title: Telegram 270, Section Two: Comments on Japan’s 1942 Food Position
subfiles.about: Transmits Penrose’s comments on a British Ministry of Economic Warfare assessment of Japan’s food position.
subfiles.summary: Penrose generally endorses the memorandum’s quantitative method and rejects predictions of an early Japanese economic collapse, while questioning whether sweeping rationing and compulsory cereal-mixing measures could be administered rapidly. He stresses that Japan proper is not food self-sufficient and depends heavily on maritime traffic from Bangkok, Saigon, and Taiwan, as well as nearby supplies from Korea and Manchuria. Disruption of these supply routes could seriously worsen the food situation.

subfiles.title: Telegram 270, Section One: Summary of the Ministry of Economic Warfare Food Study
subfiles.about: Summarizes the conclusions of a secret British study of Japan’s expected 1942 food supply.
subfiles.summary: The study estimates Japan proper’s rice requirement at roughly 10.5 million tons and the available supply from Japan, Korea, and Taiwan at about 9.7 million tons, supplemented by substantial carry-over stocks. It judges that good secondary crops and retained stocks of fish, soybeans, and sugar should permit adequate food supplies without drastic changes in living standards. Loss of imports from Taiwan, Indochina, and Thailand would require enforced economies, while the treatment of farmers and availability of fertilizers would determine the longer-term position.

subfiles.title: Telegram 272, Section Two: Raw Materials Obtainable from Thailand and Indochina
subfiles.about: Reports a British assessment of strategic materials Japan could obtain from Thailand and Indochina.
subfiles.summary: The telegram lists possible supplies of tin, tungsten, anthracite coal, zinc, salt, hides, teak, and possibly bauxite. It concludes that the territories would not remedy Japan’s major deficiencies in oil, nickel, copper, iron ore, or lead. The Ministry of Economic Warfare requests American comments where U.S. information differs.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Economic Warfare Intelligence Series No. 124
subfiles.about: Points to a paper on the effects of the Far Eastern war on Japanese and Allied food supplies.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records the subject of Economic Warfare Intelligence Series No. 124. It directs researchers to the original item filed under 740.0011 Pacific War/2403.

subfiles.title: Letter Transmitting OSS Situation Report No. 7
subfiles.from: William L. Langer, Office of Strategic Services
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a confidential OSS report on the importance of salt in the Sino-Japanese struggle.
subfiles.summary: William L. Langer sends Maxwell Hamilton a copy of Situation Report No. 7, titled “The Importance of Salt in the Economy of the Sino-Japanese Struggle.” The report was prepared by the OSS Research and Analysis Branch and classified confidential.

subfiles.title: Memorandum Summarizing Tokyo’s April 15 Foodstuffs Despatch
subfiles.about: Summarizes an embassy report on rice, canned goods, fish, soybeans, and shipping in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum estimates imperial rice supplies at 96.6 million koku against minimum demand of 100 million and anticipates a poor 1942 crop because of fertilizer shortages. It notes canned-goods reserves but acute shortages of fish and soybean products, with official pricing and transportation failures worsening distribution. Japan is described as suffering a moderate rather than catastrophic food shortage whose course depends chiefly on shipping, including possible imports of ten million koku of Southeast Asian rice.

subfiles.title: Despatch Transmitting a General Résumé of the Foodstuffs Situation in Japan Proper
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards Donald W. Lamm’s report on Japan’s food situation from December 1941 through April 1942.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew submits a report prepared by Vice Consul Donald W. Lamm of the embassy’s Reporting Section. He acknowledges Language Officer David Ray’s translations of Japanese press articles used in the report. The enclosure concerns food conditions in Japan proper during the first four months of war with the United States and Great Britain.

subfiles.title: General Résumé of the Foodstuffs Situation in Japan Proper, December 1941–April 1942
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy, Tokyo; Department of State
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s early wartime supplies of rice, canned goods, fish, soybeans, and sugar.
subfiles.summary: The report finds a pre-existing moderate food shortage worsened by poor crops, fertilizer and labor shortages, restricted fishing, and inadequate shipping from conquered territories. It contrasts optimistic foreign propaganda with domestic warnings, calculates a rice deficit, and discusses tightened rationing and the possible effect of Allied submarines on imports and fishing. Separate sections describe accumulated canned goods, fish-market disruption caused by fuel scarcity and price controls, disappearing soybean products, and sugar supplies constrained more by transport than total availability. It concludes that Japan was not near starvation but remained highly dependent on maintaining shipping.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on “Japan’s Foodstuff Position”
subfiles.about: Comments on Donald W. Lamm’s comprehensive report prepared for the War Department.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum characterizes Lamm’s report as an excellent and exhaustive survey of Japanese food problems. It quotes the report’s conclusion that Japan could continue several more years of war, even without Southeast Asian imports, because of large rice stocks and an expected minimum domestic crop of roughly 17.5–19 billion pounds.

subfiles.title: War Department Circular Transmitting “Japan’s Foodstuff Position”
subfiles.from: Truman M. Martin, Military Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: Board of Economic Warfare; Office of Strategic Services; Department of Agriculture; Department of State; O. Cumbel; Department of Commerce; Operational Intelligence A-2; Office of Naval Intelligence; Military Intelligence Service units
subfiles.about: Distributes Donald W. Lamm’s food-position study to interested wartime agencies.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Truman M. Martin forwards a paper prepared for the Military Intelligence Service by Donald W. Lamm with State Department permission. The enclosed report is dated February 5, 1943 and is circulated under a strictly confidential classification.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Foodstuff Position
subfiles.about: Provides a comprehensive statistical and analytical survey of Japan’s wartime food resources and controls.
subfiles.summary: The report argues that rice and fish were the decisive foods, with wheat, barley, sugar, and soybeans of secondary importance, and identifies labor, shipping, and fertilizer as Japan’s main agricultural constraints. It reviews the development of compulsory procurement and rationing, estimates rice production, imports, stocks, and consumption in Japan, Korea, and Taiwan, and concludes that unusually large rice reserves could sustain Japan for several years even if Southeast Asian imports ceased. Further sections analyze wheat and barley, sugar, beans, potatoes, vegetables, fruit, meat, dairy products, tea, salt, canned foods, and trade, supported by extensive statistical tables. Although shortages would narrow and simplify the civilian diet, the author expects Japan to remain broadly capable of feeding its population unless production or transportation suffered major disruption.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Vitamin Preparations and Medicines
subfiles.about: References information that Japanese food shortages were worsening and available food lacked vitamins.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference notes a report that food scarcity in Japan was being felt increasingly. It adds that available supplies were badly deficient in vitamins and points to the original paper in another file.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Scarcity of Food and Medicines in Japan
subfiles.about: Records the Enemy Branch’s interest in a prior letter about Japanese shortages of food and medicine.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references the subject submitted in an August 28 letter. It states that the matter was of particular interest to the Enemy Branch, which was following food and medical conditions for the armed forces.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Swedish Vitamin and Medicine Shipment aboard Gripsholm
subfiles.about: References a Swedish request to import vitamin preparations and medicines for its Tokyo legation aboard Gripsholm.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records that the Swedish Legation in Washington requested permission to ship vitamins and medicines to the Swedish Legation in Tokyo aboard Gripsholm. It directs the reader to the original document in file 701.5894/11.

subfiles.title: Telegram 7190: Japanese and Foreign Civilian Rations
subfiles.about: Reports German press information on food, fuel, and housing allocations in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram lists daily or monthly allowances of rice, bread, flour, sugar, meat, fish, vegetables, oil, rice wine, and occasional fruit, noting several privileges for foreigners. German organizations reportedly supplemented their nationals’ rations with small amounts of canned meat, marmalade, and fruit. The second page gives controlled rents and compares winter coal, briquette, and charcoal allocations for Europeans and Japanese.

subfiles.title: Telegram 8189: Creation of a Permanent Japanese Food Council
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese cabinet’s establishment of a council to coordinate imperial food production and distribution.
subfiles.summary: A Berlin newspaper reports that the Japanese cabinet approved a permanent food council covering Japan, Manchuria, Korea, and Taiwan. Representatives of several ministries would coordinate existing regulations and pursue food self-sufficiency under the joint leadership of the agriculture and commerce ministers. Japan and Manchuria were expected to provide capital, materials, and labor for higher production.

subfiles.title: Telegram 291: Food Autarky and Agricultural Development in Occupied Territories
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese efforts to create food self-sufficiency across the empire and occupied territories.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports agricultural schools and demonstration centers in Malaya, Sumatra, Borneo, and Celebes, together with a Makassar research institute covering agriculture, forestry, fisheries, geology, and mineralogy. Japan also planned to divide former company plantations among local cultivators, provide seed and machinery, and combat insect pests in occupied China. A renewed agreement with Indochina provided for 1944 deliveries of rice and by-products at slightly higher prices.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3017 Transmitting “Food Problems under Decisive Battle”
subfiles.about: Forwards a translation of a Japanese symposium on wartime food problems.
subfiles.summary: The embassy transmits a translation prepared by the American Co-ordinated Translation Center of an article published in the May 1, 1944 issue of Chuo Koron. Its summary highlights admitted failures in food distribution, shortages of fertilizer and livestock feed, reduced fish supplies, and the prospect of increasing grain output through better seeds. It also calls attention to official recognition of public dissatisfaction and proposals to mix sweet potatoes, corn, grass, and other materials into flour and bread.

subfiles.title: Food Problems under Decisive Battle: A Symposium
subfiles.from: Chuo Koron; translated by the Co-ordinated Translation Center, Chungking
subfiles.to: Foreign Economic Administration and other U.S. agencies
subfiles.about: Presents Japanese agricultural officials’ discussion of procurement, distribution, fertilizers, animal feed, land improvement, seeds, fish, and soybeans.
subfiles.summary: Officials describe replacing individual rice-delivery obligations with community responsibility, earlier procurement quotas, and stronger involvement by local governments and agricultural associations. They acknowledge the difficulty of coordinating staple and subsidiary foods and propose linking production plans to distribution of fish, vegetables, and other perishables. The discussion advocates farm-produced manure, decentralized livestock raising, clearer separation of human food from animal feed, cultivation of unused land, improved fertilizer efficiency, and wider adoption of high-yield seed. Faced with falling fish supplies, Yukawa identifies Manchurian soybeans as a major substitute source of protein; the translated symposium continues beyond page 72.
